title: The Cave of Adullam and the Massacre at Nob
summary: David hides in the cave of Adullam, where his family and about four hundred distressed, indebted, and discontented men gather to him. He shelters his parents with the king of Moab and, on the word of the prophet Gad, returns to Judah. Meanwhile Saul accuses his servants of conspiracy, and Doeg the Edomite reports that Ahimelech helped David. Saul orders the priests killed; when his own guards refuse, Doeg slaughters eighty-five priests and destroys the town of Nob. Only Abiathar escapes, and David takes responsibility and promises to protect him.
story: In chapter 21 David was alone, hungry, and pretending madness among the Philistines. Chapter 22 shows two kingdoms taking shape. Around David gathers a band of outcasts, a prophet (Gad), and, by the end of the chapter, a priest (Abiathar) with the ephod. Around Saul gather suspicion, informers, and a foreign henchman who kills the priests of the LORD. The contrast is stark: the rejected king destroys the priesthood, while the anointed fugitive receives its survivor. This chapter also fulfills the grim word spoken against the house of Eli in 2:31-33, since the priests of Nob were Eli's descendants.
historical:
Adullam was a town in the lowlands of Judah, southwest of Bethlehem, not far from the Valley of Elah; the region is full of limestone caves. The headings of Psalms 57 and 142 connect those psalms with David's time in a cave, either here or at En-gedi (chapter 24). Mizpeh of Moab is unidentified, but Moab lay east of the Dead Sea. David's choice of Moab as a refuge for his parents makes sense given his family history: according to Ruth 4:13-22, his great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite. It may also reflect Moab's hostility toward Saul, who had fought against Moab (14:47).

Gad the prophet appears here for the first time and later serves David as king (2 Samuel 24:11; 1 Chronicles 29:29). Doeg the Edomite, seen at Nob in chapter 21, now acts as informer and executioner. The heading of Psalm 52 connects that psalm with Doeg's report to Saul, and its description of a man who trusts in destruction and loves evil more than good fits this chapter.
cultural:
The men who gather to David are described by their circumstances: people under pressure, people in debt, and people bitter in spirit. In the ancient Near East such people often left settled society and formed bands on the margins, living by raiding or by hiring themselves out for protection. David's band follows that pattern, but under his leadership it becomes the core of a future royal army. The "stronghold" (verses 4 and 5) was a natural fortress in rough country, a place of defense rather than a built castle.

Saul's speech to his servants appeals to tribal loyalty: he addresses them as men of Benjamin, his own tribe, and asks whether David, a man of Judah, would give them fields and commands as Saul has. Royal patronage (land grants and military posts) was how ancient kings secured loyalty. The linen ephod worn by the priests was a simple priestly garment, distinct from the high priest's ornate ephod. Killing priests was a shocking act; Saul's own guards refuse to strike them, and he has to turn to a foreigner.
literary: The chapter alternates between David and Saul. It opens with David gathering people (verses 1 to 5), shifts to Saul accusing people (verses 6 to 19), and returns to David receiving the survivor (verses 20 to 23). The pictures of the two leaders are carefully drawn: Saul sits under a tree with a spear in his hand, surrounded by servants he suspects; David stands in a cave surrounded by people who have nowhere else to go. Ahimelech's defense of David (verse 14) is the only full statement of David's loyalty anywhere in Saul's court, and it gets him killed. The list of victims in verse 19 (men and women, children and infants, oxen, donkeys, and sheep) deliberately echoes the command about Amalek in 15:3, so that Saul carries out against the priests of the LORD the total destruction he failed to carry out against Amalek.

outline.t: The cave of Adullam: David's company of the distressed
David's parents in Moab; Gad's word to return to Judah
Doeg slaughters the priests and destroys Nob

doctrines.note: The massacre at Nob fulfills the word against Eli's house (2:31-33; compare 1 Kings 2:27), yet Saul and Doeg bear full guilt for it. The chapter holds together God's judgment and human responsibility without explaining away either.

David's band is made up of the distressed, the indebted, and the discontented. God's people have often been formed from the margins rather than the center, a pattern visible in Israel's beginnings as slaves and in the first followers of Jesus.
Saul's suspicion turns to paranoia, and paranoia to murder. He accuses his own son and servants, then kills the priests of the LORD. The chapter shows the end of a heart that will not submit to God.

words.note: Qashar, to conspire, literally to bind together. Saul uses it twice, of his servants and of Ahimelech. The word reveals Saul's mindset: he sees plots everywhere, while the text shows that no one is plotting against him.

Aman, to be faithful or reliable, the root from which comes "amen." Ahimelech asks who is as faithful as David. It is the truest thing said in Saul's presence in the chapter, and the king answers it with a death sentence.

Metsudah, stronghold or fortress. A natural refuge in rugged terrain. The same word recurs in the Psalms, where the LORD himself is called a fortress, a connection many readers have drawn to David's years of hiding.

Mishmeret, charge or safekeeping. In verse 23 David tells Abiathar he will be safe with him, literally that he will be in David's charge. David accepts responsibility for the survivor, taking on the protection his own deception failed to give Abiathar's family.

christ: Jesus gathered around himself people who had little standing, including tax collectors, sinners, and the poor, and he said he had come for the sick rather than the healthy (Mark 2:17). The picture of David's band at Adullam is a thematic anticipation of that, not a prediction: the true king is hidden and hunted, and those who come to him are those with nowhere else to go. David's promise to Abiathar, that the one who seeks his life seeks David's as well and that he will be safe with him, also sounds a note the gospel develops: the king binds his own life to the lives of those who take refuge with him.

hard.q: Why did God allow the innocent priests of Nob and their families to be slaughtered?
hard.a: The chapter does not soften this atrocity or offer an easy explanation. Several things can be said. The text places guilt squarely on Saul and Doeg, and implicitly acknowledges David's part through his confession in verse 22. It also recalls the long-announced judgment on Eli's house (2:27-36), which suggests that God's purposes were at work even in this evil, but without making the killers any less guilty. Some readers find that framework troubling, since the victims include children who had no part in Eli's sins; others note that the Old Testament often speaks of consequences falling on families and communities while also insisting that each person is judged for their own sin (Ezekiel 18). The chapter's own response is lament and protection: David takes responsibility, grieves, and shelters the survivor. It does not ask the reader to call the slaughter good.

questions: David's company was made up of the distressed, the indebted, and the discontented. What does this suggest about the kind of people God uses to build his kingdom?
David said, "I myself am responsible." How do you respond when your actions have harmed others, even unintentionally?
Saul's servants refused to kill the priests. When have you faced pressure from someone in authority to do what you knew was wrong?
